subject: Computer Networking
title: Access Points Explained
description: A micro-lesson that makes Access Points Explained usable.

hook.text: Office Wi-Fi doesn't come from a router. It comes from dedicated access points on the ceiling.

buildup.text: An access point bridges wireless clients to the wired network. It converts Wi-Fi frames to Ethernet.

discovery.text: Enterprise APs handle hundreds of clients at once with band steering and airtime fairness.

twist.text: One AP broadcasts multiple SSIDs — employees, guests, IoT — each on a different VLAN.

climax.text: Wireless controllers manage hundreds of APs centrally. One dashboard for channels, power, and security.

punchline.text: Access points serve Wi-Fi. Controllers make them a team.

quiz.question: What does band steering do on an access point?
options: Guides devices to the less congested frequency band
Increases the transmit power of the AP

details.summary: A wireless access point connects Wi-Fi devices to a wired network, converting radio signals to Ethernet frames and vice versa. Enterprise access points support multiple SSIDs, band steering, fast roaming, and centralized management across hundreds of units.
details.whyItMatters: Access points are the bridge between wireless devices and the wired network backbone. Proper placement and configuration directly determine Wi-Fi coverage, speed, and reliability.
takeaways: Access points bridge wireless devices to the wired network
Enterprise APs support central management and fast roaming
Band steering directs capable devices to faster frequencies

faq.question: What is the difference between an access point and a router?
faq.answer: A router connects different networks and assigns IP addresses. An access point only bridges wireless devices to an existing wired network. Home routers include a built-in access point, but enterprises use separate dedicated APs managed by a wireless controller.

faq.question: How many access points does a building need?
faq.answer: Coverage depends on building materials, layout, and user density. A typical office needs one access point per 1,500 to 2,500 square feet. Concrete walls and high-density areas require more. A professional site survey with heat mapping determines optimal placement.
